title: The linear twin

data.source: Muth (1960); steady-state Kalman filter; ARMA theory (Box and Jenkins); cumulants of linear processes (Brillinger, Rosenblatt); cited from memory. Simulated chains, exact inverse Gaussian sampling, seeded.

prediction: A seed world and an enduring world give the same list of gaps exactly at second order whenever the seed pulls in a straight line, and at every order only when the noise is Gaussian; with lopsided noise, and so for true first-passage gaps, the third-order number D3 is not zero and the seed world can be told apart from every linear enduring world (one hidden number moving by a fixed fraction plus independent luck, read with independent additive luck).
baseline: ARMA(1,1) theory and the cumulants of linear processes. Null for the joint law: two runs of the same world, and shuffled chains. Decoy: the Gaussian twin read through a monotone dial.
relation: equivalent at second order; equivalent at all orders only in the Gaussian case
status_line: CRR here is: the same as an enduring hidden state at second order, exactly so only for Gaussian noise; with first-passage gaps the simple twin fails at third order.
why: The autocorrelations of the first-passage seed world sit on the ARMA(1,1) values, as the short argument says they must. The third-order number D3 is zero for every linear enduring world (an AR(1) state with independent additive reading noise) and is not zero here. The joint law of two successive gaps differs from the Gaussian twin even after the twin is given the same single-gap law. This compares two descriptions of a simulated list; it says nothing about which the world uses. An enduring world with a richer hidden state can still copy a seed world exactly.
